title_options: Why You Fall For Things You See A Lot
This Is Why Ads Work On You
Your Brain Is Tricking You Right Now

segments.voiceover: You don't like this song because it's good. You like it because you've heard it 50 times.
segments.visual_prompt: close up of a person listening to music with headphones, neon lights, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the mere-exposure effect.
segments.visual_prompt: radio playing in a car dashboard, vertical

segments.voiceover: The more your brain sees or hears something, the safer it feels. Familiar equals safe. Safe equals liked.
segments.visual_prompt: brain scan animation glowing blue, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why brands repeat the same ad. Why exes seem better with time. Why you hum songs you used to hate.
segments.visual_prompt: billboard advertisement repeating on a city street, vertical

segments.voiceover: You don't like this. You're just used to it. Now go check your playlist.
segments.visual_prompt: phone screen showing a music app playlist, vertical

caption: Your brain is way easier to hack than you think. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why Unfinished Tasks Haunt You
The Reason You Can't Stop Thinking About It
This Is Why Netflix Uses Cliffhangers

segments.voiceover: Ever notice how an unfinished text argument lives in your head rent free? There's a reason.
segments.visual_prompt: person staring at phone anxiously in bed at night, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: WHY YOU CAN'T LET IT GO

segments.voiceover: It's called the Zeigarnik effect.
segments.visual_prompt: close up of a clock ticking, vertical

segments.voiceover: Your brain hates open loops. Finished tasks get filed away. Unfinished ones stay loud, on purpose.
segments.visual_prompt: open file folders scattered on a desk, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why cliffhangers work. Why unread messages annoy you. Why you remember the fight, not the apology.
segments.visual_prompt: tv screen showing a cliffhanger scene, vertical

segments.voiceover: So next time something won't leave your head, just finish it. Now go check, what's still open in your head right now?
segments.visual_prompt: person writing final checkmark on a to-do list, vertical

caption: This is literally why you replay that one conversation. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why Attractive People Get Away With More
This Bias Controls How You Judge People
You Are Not As Objective As You Think

segments.voiceover: Attractive people get hired faster, trusted more, and forgiven quicker. It's not fair, and it's not random.
segments.visual_prompt: confident person walking into a job interview, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: IT'S NOT FAIR. IT'S A BIAS

segments.voiceover: It's called the halo effect.
segments.visual_prompt: golden light glowing around a silhouette, vertical

segments.voiceover: One good trait, like looks, makes your brain assume other good traits exist too. Smarter, kinder, more honest.
segments.visual_prompt: close up of eyes scanning a face, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's why tall people seem more competent. Why well-dressed people seem more trustworthy. None of it is proof.
segments.visual_prompt: person in a suit shaking hands confidently, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's not fair. It's a bias. Now think about the last person you trusted instantly, why did you really trust them?
segments.visual_prompt: two people meeting for the first time, handshake close up, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: WHO DID YOU TRUST TOO FAST?

caption: One good trait is quietly deciding how people see you. #psychologyfacts

title_options: The Trick Salespeople Use On You
Why Small Yeses Lead To Big Ones
This Is How You Get Manipulated Slowly

segments.voiceover: Someone asks you for a tiny favor. You say yes. Weeks later you're doing something way bigger for them.
segments.visual_prompt: person signing a small form at a door, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called foot-in-the-door.
segments.visual_prompt: close up of a foot stopping a closing door, vertical

segments.voiceover: Once you agree to something small, your brain rewrites your identity. You're now, the type of person who helps.
segments.visual_prompt: brain animation rewriting neural pathways, vertical

segments.voiceover: So the next ask feels consistent, not manipulative. Salespeople know this. So do controlling friends.
segments.visual_prompt: salesperson smiling at a front door with a clipboard, vertical

segments.voiceover: It starts small. That's the whole trick. So next time, ask yourself what the first small yes was.
segments.visual_prompt: person closing a door thoughtfully, vertical

caption: This is how you end up agreeing to things you never wanted. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why Big Asks Get You A Yes Later
The Reverse Trick That Works On Everyone
This Negotiation Hack Is Sneaky

segments.voiceover: Someone asks for something huge. You say no. Then they ask for something smaller, and you say yes instantly.
segments.visual_prompt: person shaking their head no at a negotiation table, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called door-in-the-face.
segments.visual_prompt: door slamming shut in slow motion, vertical

segments.voiceover: The big ask was never real. It exists to make the real ask feel small by comparison.
segments.visual_prompt: scale comparing a big object and a small object, vertical

segments.voiceover: Your brain feels relief saying yes to the smaller one. Relief feels like a good decision. It's not.
segments.visual_prompt: person exhaling relief after a decision, vertical

segments.voiceover: You just got played, and it felt like a win. Now think, when was the last time saying no made you agree faster later?
segments.visual_prompt: two people finalizing a deal with a handshake, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: WHEN DID THIS HAPPEN TO YOU?

caption: Negotiators use this constantly. Now you'll spot it every time. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why You're Always 'Right' In Arguments
Your Brain Is Lying To You On Purpose
This Bias Ruins Every Debate You Have

segments.voiceover: You're not actually looking for the truth. You're looking for proof that you were right all along.
segments.visual_prompt: person scrolling phone news feed intensely, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called confirmation bias.
segments.visual_prompt: magnifying glass over a newspaper headline, vertical

segments.voiceover: Your brain seeks out information that agrees with what you already believe, and quietly ignores the rest.
segments.visual_prompt: person ignoring one book and picking another from a shelf, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why two people can watch the same debate and both walk away feeling like they won.
segments.visual_prompt: two people watching a tv debate with different reactions, vertical

segments.voiceover: Your brain is lying to you, and it feels completely true. So next time you're 'right', ask what you didn't search for.
segments.visual_prompt: person closing a laptop after research, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: WHAT DID YOU NOT SEARCH FOR?

caption: The reason every side of every argument feels 'obviously right'. #psychologyfacts

title_options: The Limit On How Many Friends You Can Have
Why You Can't Keep Up With Everyone
Your Brain Has A Friendship Cap

segments.voiceover: You have 800 followers, but your brain can only actually handle about 150 real relationships. Here's why.
segments.visual_prompt: phone screen showing a large contacts list scrolling fast, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called Dunbar's number.
segments.visual_prompt: group of friends silhouettes standing together, vertical

segments.voiceover: An anthropologist found our brains are wired to maintain roughly 150 stable relationships, max. Not more.
segments.visual_prompt: brain size comparison illustration, vertical

segments.voiceover: Past that, people become names, not relationships. That's why huge friend groups always have inner circles.
segments.visual_prompt: crowd of people blurred except a small group in focus, vertical

segments.voiceover: Quality beats quantity, your brain already decided that for you. Now go count who's actually in your 150.
segments.visual_prompt: small close friend group laughing together, vertical

caption: This is why you feel closer to 5 people than to 500 followers. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why You Copy People Without Noticing
The Reason You Like People Who Mirror You
Your Body Is Copying Strangers Right Now

segments.voiceover: Watch two close friends talk. They'll cross their arms at the same time, without either one noticing.
segments.visual_prompt: two friends talking and mirroring body language, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the chameleon effect.
segments.visual_prompt: chameleon changing color close up, vertical

segments.voiceover: We unconsciously mimic the posture, tone, and gestures of people we like or want to bond with.
segments.visual_prompt: two people leaning in the same direction at a table, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's automatic, and it works both ways. Mirror someone on purpose, and they'll like you more, instantly.
segments.visual_prompt: person subtly copying another person's hand gesture, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: MIRROR THEM, THEY LIKE YOU MORE

segments.voiceover: You've been doing this your whole life without noticing. Now go watch your next conversation happen in real time.
segments.visual_prompt: group of friends sitting in similar poses at a cafe, vertical

caption: Try mirroring someone on purpose today and watch what happens. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why Nobody Helps In A Crowd
The More Witnesses, The Less Help You Get
This Is Why You Freeze In Public

segments.voiceover: Someone collapses in a crowded street. The bigger the crowd, the less likely anyone helps. That's backwards, right?
segments.visual_prompt: crowded city street with people walking past, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the bystander effect.
segments.visual_prompt: crowd standing around watching something, vertical

segments.voiceover: When responsibility is shared by everyone, it feels owned by no one. Each person assumes someone else will act.
segments.visual_prompt: circle of people looking at each other, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why one person alone will help almost every time, but a crowd of 20 often does nothing.
segments.visual_prompt: one person stepping forward to help from a group, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: ALONE, YOU ACT. IN A CROWD, YOU FREEZE

segments.voiceover: So if you ever need help in public, point at one person directly. Now you'll never freeze in a crowd again.
segments.visual_prompt: person pointing directly at someone specific in a crowd, vertical

caption: Save this. It could actually matter one day. #psychologyfacts

title_options: The Number That Controls Your Decisions
Why The First Price You See Traps You
This Is How Stores Manipulate Your Brain

segments.voiceover: A shirt is 90 dollars. Crossed out, now 45. You feel like you're winning. You're not.
segments.visual_prompt: price tag with a crossed out discount in a store, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called anchoring bias.
segments.visual_prompt: ship anchor dropping into water, vertical

segments.voiceover: The first number you see becomes the reference point for every judgment after it, even if it was made up.
segments.visual_prompt: number scale with a marker fixed at one point, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why stores show the 'original price' first. Why salary negotiations start high. Anchors control the whole conversation.
segments.visual_prompt: shopping mall storefront with sale signs, vertical

segments.voiceover: You're not getting a deal, you're getting anchored. Now go check the last 'discount' you fell for.
segments.visual_prompt: person checking a receipt outside a store, vertical

caption: This is why nothing feels expensive after seeing the 'original price'. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why Losing Hurts More Than Winning Feels Good
This Bias Controls Every Decision You Make
Your Brain Fears Loss Twice As Much

segments.voiceover: Losing 50 dollars hurts about twice as much as finding 50 dollars feels good. Your brain is wired unfairly.
segments.visual_prompt: person dropping and losing cash on the street, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called loss aversion.
segments.visual_prompt: scale tipping heavily to one side, vertical

segments.voiceover: Evolution made losses feel bigger than gains, because losing resources once meant death, not inconvenience.
segments.visual_prompt: ancient cave silhouette, survival themed, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why you stay in bad jobs, bad relationships, and losing stocks. Leaving feels like a loss, staying feels safe.
segments.visual_prompt: person hesitating at a fork in the road, vertical

segments.voiceover: Losing hurts twice as much, so your brain lies to keep you stuck. Now think, what are you avoiding losing right now?
segments.visual_prompt: person walking away confidently from an old path, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: WHAT ARE YOU AFRAID TO LOSE?

caption: This is why quitting anything feels harder than it should. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why First Impressions Basically Never Change
The Reason You Can't Forget How You Met Someone
Your Brain Locks In The First Few Seconds

segments.voiceover: You decide if you like someone in about seven seconds. Everything after that is just your brain confirming it.
segments.visual_prompt: two strangers making eye contact for the first time, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the primacy effect.
segments.visual_prompt: clock counting down seconds, vertical

segments.voiceover: Information you get first gets stored deeper in memory, and shapes how you interpret everything that follows.
segments.visual_prompt: filing cabinet drawer opening with the first folder highlighted, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why a bad first impression is so hard to undo. You're not judging them anymore, you're judging your first memory of them.
segments.visual_prompt: person trying to rebuild trust after a bad start, vertical

segments.voiceover: Seven seconds decide everything, so make yours count. Now think about the first impression you made today.
segments.visual_prompt: person confidently walking into a room, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: WHAT WAS YOUR FIRST SEVEN SECONDS TODAY?

caption: This is why you still remember exactly how you met your best friend. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why You Only Remember The Last Thing Someone Said
This Is Why Endings Matter More Than You Think
Your Memory Plays Favorites With Time

segments.voiceover: A five-star date can be ruined by one awkward last minute. Your brain remembers endings the loudest.
segments.visual_prompt: couple saying goodbye awkwardly at a doorway, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the recency effect.
segments.visual_prompt: hourglass with sand running out, vertical

segments.voiceover: The most recent information is the freshest in memory, so it gets weighted heavier than everything before it.
segments.visual_prompt: brain highlighting the last item in a sequence, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why job interviewers remember your last answer best. Why the last slide of a presentation matters most.
segments.visual_prompt: interview room, person answering final question, vertical

segments.voiceover: Endings matter more than you think, so always finish strong. Now think about how you ended your last conversation.
segments.visual_prompt: person leaving a meeting with a confident smile, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: HOW DID YOU END YOUR LAST TALK?

caption: This is why you should never end a text on a bad note. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why Horoscopes Feel So Accurate
The Trick Psychics Use On Everyone
This Is Why Vague Statements Feel Personal

segments.voiceover: Your horoscope isn't reading your future. It's reading a sentence vague enough to fit anyone alive.
segments.visual_prompt: person reading horoscope on phone in bed, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the Barnum effect.
segments.visual_prompt: fortune teller card spread on a table, vertical

segments.voiceover: Statements so general, like 'you seem confident but sometimes doubt yourself', feel personal because they fit almost everyone.
segments.visual_prompt: close up of a printed generic personality description, vertical

segments.voiceover: Your brain fills in the specific details from your own life, then credits the horoscope for the accuracy.
segments.visual_prompt: person nodding while reading something on a phone, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: YOUR BRAIN FILLS IN THE GAPS

segments.voiceover: It's not magic, it's just vague enough to fit anyone. Now go reread today's horoscope and count the vague words.
segments.visual_prompt: phone screen showing a daily horoscope app, vertical

caption: Sorry, but Mercury has nothing to do with it. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why You Overvalue Things You Build Yourself
This Is Why DIY Furniture Feels Priceless
Your Effort Is Tricking Your Own Judgment

segments.voiceover: You'll defend that wobbly shelf you built for an hour, over a better one you could buy in five minutes.
segments.visual_prompt: person assembling flat-pack furniture with tools, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: YOU BUILT IT, YOU LOVE IT

segments.voiceover: It's called the IKEA effect.
segments.visual_prompt: furniture assembly instructions and tools on the floor, vertical

segments.voiceover: Effort creates ownership, and ownership creates emotional value, even if the object itself is objectively worse.
segments.visual_prompt: person admiring a finished piece of furniture, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why you value your own ideas more than better ones. Why homemade gifts feel bigger than expensive ones.
segments.visual_prompt: handmade gift being wrapped, vertical

segments.voiceover: You built it, so of course you love it. Now think about the last thing you overvalued just because you made it.
segments.visual_prompt: person proudly showing something they made, vertical

caption: This is why that wobbly shelf is staying forever. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why More Options Make You Less Happy
This Is Why Netflix Stresses You Out
Too Many Choices Are Ruining Your Brain

segments.voiceover: You spend twenty minutes scrolling Netflix, pick nothing, and go to bed stressed. Sound familiar?
segments.visual_prompt: person scrolling through streaming app menu endlessly, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the paradox of choice.
segments.visual_prompt: grocery aisle with hundreds of similar products, vertical

segments.voiceover: More options should mean more freedom, but past a point, your brain gets overwhelmed and satisfaction actually drops.
segments.visual_prompt: brain overloaded animation with many arrows, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why you're happier picking from three restaurants than from thirty. Fewer options, faster decisions, more peace.
segments.visual_prompt: person happily choosing from a small simple menu, vertical

segments.voiceover: Too many options aren't freedom, they're stress. Now go pick the first decent option you see today.
segments.visual_prompt: person confidently closing a menu after deciding, vertical

caption: This is scientifically why you can't pick a show to watch. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why You Judge Whole Trips By One Moment
This Is How Your Memory Actually Works
Your Brain Ignores Most Of Your Life

segments.voiceover: A ten day vacation gets remembered by two moments. The best one, and the last one. The rest basically vanishes.
segments.visual_prompt: person looking through vacation photos on a phone, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: YOUR BRAIN DELETES MOST OF IT

segments.voiceover: It's called the peak-end rule.
segments.visual_prompt: mountain peak with a sunset ending the day, vertical

segments.voiceover: We don't remember experiences as a whole. We remember the most intense moment, and how it ended, nothing more.
segments.visual_prompt: timeline graphic highlighting a peak and an end point, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why a rough flight delay doesn't ruin a trip if the last night was amazing. Endings rewrite the story.
segments.visual_prompt: person smiling at an airport gate despite a delay, vertical

segments.voiceover: Your brain deletes most of your life and keeps two moments. Now make sure the ending is a good one.
segments.visual_prompt: sunset over a beach, peaceful ending shot, vertical

caption: This is why the last day of a trip matters more than day three. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why You Finish Bad Movies You Hate
This Bias Keeps You Stuck In The Wrong Things
Your Past Spending Is Trapping Your Future

segments.voiceover: You hate the movie. You paid for the ticket. So you sit there for two more hours anyway. Why?
segments.visual_prompt: bored person watching a movie in a theater, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the sunk cost fallacy.
segments.visual_prompt: money and a ticket stub being thrown into a fire, vertical

segments.voiceover: You keep investing in something just to justify what you already spent, even when leaving is clearly better.
segments.visual_prompt: person pouring more money into a broken machine, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: PAST SPENDING ISN'T A REASON TO STAY

segments.voiceover: That's why you stay in bad relationships after years invested. Why you finish degrees you no longer want. The past can't be recovered by staying.
segments.visual_prompt: person standing at a crossroad holding an old photo, vertical

segments.voiceover: The money's already gone either way. Now think, what are you still finishing just because you started it?
segments.visual_prompt: person walking out of a movie theater confidently mid-film, vertical

caption: This is why quitting the bad thing is always the right move. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Nobody Is Looking At You As Much As You Think
Why You're Not As Watched As You Feel
This Is Why Embarrassment Feels Bigger Than It Is

segments.voiceover: You trip in public and think everyone saw. In reality, most people didn't even look up from their phones.
segments.visual_prompt: person tripping slightly on a busy sidewalk, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the spotlight effect.
segments.visual_prompt: spotlight shining on a single person in a crowd, vertical

segments.voiceover: You overestimate how much people notice you, because you're the main character of your own mind, not theirs.
segments.visual_prompt: person imagining themselves under a spotlight while crowd ignores them, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: YOU'RE ONLY THE MAIN CHARACTER TO YOU

segments.voiceover: Studies show people notice about half of what you think they do, and forget it within minutes.
segments.visual_prompt: people walking past each other, absorbed in their own phones, vertical

segments.voiceover: Nobody's watching as closely as you think. Now go do the thing you were too embarrassed to do.
segments.visual_prompt: person confidently walking forward, head up, vertical

caption: That embarrassing moment you replay? Nobody else remembers it. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why Small Mistakes Make People Like You More
This Is Why 'Perfect' People Feel Cold
A Little Clumsiness Is A Secret Weapon

segments.voiceover: A competent person spills their coffee, and suddenly people like them more, not less. That's not random.
segments.visual_prompt: person laughing after spilling coffee at a cafe, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the pratfall effect.
segments.visual_prompt: someone slipping slightly but recovering with a laugh, vertical

segments.voiceover: Small, harmless mistakes make skilled people feel human and relatable, instead of intimidating.
segments.visual_prompt: confident speaker laughing off a small mistake on stage, vertical

segments.voiceover: But it only works if you're already seen as competent. For someone unproven, the same mistake just confirms doubt.
segments.visual_prompt: two contrasting reactions to the same mistake, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: IT ONLY WORKS IF YOU'RE ALREADY GOOD

segments.voiceover: A little clumsiness is a secret weapon, not a weakness. Now stop hiding your small mistakes.
segments.visual_prompt: person laughing genuinely with others, vertical

caption: This is why the funny coworker who messes up a little is everyone's favorite. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why Free Samples Actually Work On You
The Debt You Feel After Any Small Favor
This Is How Guilt Gets Built Into Your Brain

segments.voiceover: Someone hands you a free sample. You didn't ask for it, but now you feel weirdly obligated to buy something.
segments.visual_prompt: person offering a free food sample at a store, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the reciprocity principle.
segments.visual_prompt: two hands exchanging a small gift, vertical

segments.voiceover: Humans are wired to repay favors, even tiny unrequested ones, because in our history, owing nothing meant owing everything.
segments.visual_prompt: ancient tribal trading scene illustration, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: OWING NOTHING USED TO BE DANGEROUS

segments.voiceover: That's why salespeople give things away first. Why a compliment makes you want to compliment back instantly.
segments.visual_prompt: salesperson handing over a small gift with a smile, vertical

segments.voiceover: That 'free' sample isn't free, it's a debt. Now notice the next small gift someone hands you.
segments.visual_prompt: person politely declining a free sample, vertical

caption: Free samples are a psychology hack, not generosity. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why 'Only 2 Left' Makes You Panic Buy
This Is Why Limited Time Offers Work
Your Brain Wants What It Might Lose

segments.voiceover: 'Only 2 left in stock' does more to your brain than any actual sale. You suddenly need it.
segments.visual_prompt: online store showing low stock warning on a product page, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called the scarcity principle.
segments.visual_prompt: empty shelf with one item left, vertical

segments.voiceover: Things feel more valuable the moment they might disappear, not because they changed, but because access did.
segments.visual_prompt: countdown timer on a sale banner, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: SCARCE = VALUABLE, EVEN IF NOTHING CHANGED

segments.voiceover: That's why limited time offers work, why sold-out drops go viral, why 'last chance' emails get opened instantly.
segments.visual_prompt: sold out sign on a store display, vertical

segments.voiceover: Your brain wants what it might lose, not what's actually rare. Now go check, do you actually need it?
segments.visual_prompt: person closing a checkout page and thinking twice, vertical

caption: The countdown timer is doing more work than the discount. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why You Trust Reviews More Than Your Own Eyes
This Is Why Fake Lines Actually Work
Your Brain Copies The Crowd Automatically

segments.voiceover: A restaurant with a line outside looks better than an empty one, even if the empty one has better food.
segments.visual_prompt: line of people waiting outside a restaurant at night, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called social proof.
segments.visual_prompt: five star reviews floating above a phone screen, vertical

segments.voiceover: When we're unsure what to do, we copy what everyone else is doing, assuming the crowd knows something we don't.
segments.visual_prompt: crowd of people all looking in the same direction, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why reviews sell products more than ads. Why empty restaurants stay empty, and full ones get fuller.
segments.visual_prompt: phone screen showing hundreds of product reviews, vertical

segments.voiceover: The line is the marketing, not the food. Now think about the last thing you bought just because of the reviews.
segments.visual_prompt: person adding an item to cart after reading reviews, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: WHAT DID YOU BUY FOR THE REVIEWS?

caption: This is why five stars sell more than the actual product does. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why You Defend Bad Decisions Instead Of Fixing Them
This Is Why You Lie To Yourself Daily
Your Brain Hates Admitting It Was Wrong

segments.voiceover: You bought the expensive thing you don't need. Now you defend it to everyone, including yourself.
segments.visual_prompt: person justifying an expensive purchase to a friend, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called cognitive dissonance.
segments.visual_prompt: two conflicting thought bubbles above a person's head, vertical

segments.voiceover: Holding two conflicting beliefs, like 'I'm smart' and 'I made a dumb choice', creates real mental discomfort.
segments.visual_prompt: brain animation with two clashing halves, vertical

segments.voiceover: So instead of fixing the mistake, your brain edits the story until the mistake feels smart. It's easier than admitting fault.
segments.visual_prompt: person rewriting a story in a notebook, vertical

segments.voiceover: You're defending a mistake, not the decision. Now think, what have you been justifying lately instead of just fixing?
segments.visual_prompt: person finally admitting a mistake with relief, vertical

caption: This is why nobody ever says 'yeah that was a dumb purchase'. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why You Take Credit But Never The Blame
This Bias Protects Your Ego Constantly
You're Not As Fair To Yourself As You Think

segments.voiceover: You got the promotion because you're talented. You got fired because your boss was unfair. Notice the pattern?
segments.visual_prompt: person celebrating a promotion at work, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called self-serving bias.
segments.visual_prompt: mirror reflecting a slightly flattering version of a person, vertical

segments.voiceover: We credit our successes to skill, and blame our failures on circumstances, to protect our self-image.
segments.visual_prompt: trophy on one side, storm clouds on the other, vertical

segments.voiceover: It feels honest in the moment, but it quietly stops you from learning from your actual mistakes.
segments.visual_prompt: person ignoring a mistake report on a desk, vertical

segments.voiceover: Notice the pattern, your ego is editing the story. Now think about your last failure, what part was actually you?
segments.visual_prompt: person reflecting honestly in front of a mirror, vertical

caption: Painful but true. Your ego edits your own history. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why A Sugar Pill Can Actually Heal You
This Is Proof Your Mind Controls Your Body
Belief Alone Can Change Your Biology

segments.voiceover: You take a pill with zero active ingredients, and your pain actually goes down. That's not imaginary.
segments.visual_prompt: person taking a pill with a glass of water, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: THE PILL DID NOTHING. YOU HEALED ANYWAY

segments.voiceover: It's called the placebo effect.
segments.visual_prompt: sugar pills close up in a doctor's hand, vertical

segments.voiceover: Expecting relief triggers real chemical changes in the brain, like releasing actual painkillers your body makes itself.
segments.visual_prompt: brain releasing glowing chemical signals, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's so strong that in some studies, fake surgery reduced pain almost as well as the real surgery did.
segments.visual_prompt: hospital operating room, calm and clinical, vertical

segments.voiceover: The pill did nothing, your belief did the work. Now think about what else in your life is powered by pure belief.
segments.visual_prompt: person feeling noticeably better, smiling, vertical

caption: Your mind is quietly one of the strongest drugs that exists. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why Beginners Are Often The Most Confident
This Is Why Experts Doubt Themselves More
The Less You Know, The More Sure You Feel

segments.voiceover: The person who just learned one fact is often more confident than the actual expert. That's not a coincidence.
segments.visual_prompt: confident beginner explaining something loudly, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: THE BEGINNER FEELS LIKE THE EXPERT

segments.voiceover: It's called the Dunning-Kruger effect.
segments.visual_prompt: graph showing confidence spiking early then dropping, vertical

segments.voiceover: At low skill levels, you don't know enough to see how much you don't know, so confidence peaks way too early.
segments.visual_prompt: person standing confidently at the bottom of a huge mountain, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: YOU DON'T KNOW WHAT YOU DON'T KNOW

segments.voiceover: As real skill grows, you finally see the size of the topic, and confidence actually drops before it recovers.
segments.visual_prompt: expert looking humble and thoughtful, vertical

segments.voiceover: The beginner feels like the expert, and the expert knows better. Now think, where are you overconfident right now?
segments.visual_prompt: person quietly studying, humble posture, vertical

caption: The loudest person in the room is usually the least sure, statistically. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why You Can't Put Your Phone Down
This Is The Same Trick Slot Machines Use
Your Apps Are Designed Like Casinos

segments.voiceover: You pull to refresh your feed, not knowing what's there. That uncertainty is the whole addiction.
segments.visual_prompt: close up of a thumb pulling to refresh a social media app, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called variable reward.
segments.visual_prompt: slot machine lights spinning close up, vertical

segments.voiceover: Your brain releases more dopamine from an unpredictable reward than from a guaranteed one, exactly like a slot machine.
segments.visual_prompt: brain releasing dopamine burst animation, vertical

segments.voiceover: Sometimes the post is boring, sometimes it's amazing, and you never know which, so you keep checking.
segments.visual_prompt: person endlessly scrolling phone at night, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: YOU NEVER KNOW WHICH ONE IT'LL BE

segments.voiceover: The uncertainty is the addiction, not the content. Now go turn off one notification today.
segments.visual_prompt: person turning off phone notifications in settings, vertical

caption: Your phone is designed by the same psychology as a casino. #psychologyfacts

title_options: The Two Minds Living Inside Your Head
Why You Make Bad Decisions When You're Tired
This Is How Your Brain Actually Thinks

segments.voiceover: You have two brains fighting for control right now. One is fast and lazy. One is slow and careful.
segments.visual_prompt: split screen of a fast reaction and a slow thoughtful person, vertical

segments.voiceover: Psychologists call them System 1 and System 2.
segments.visual_prompt: two glowing brain hemispheres animation, vertical

segments.voiceover: System 1 is instant, emotional, and automatic. System 2 is slow, logical, and takes real effort to switch on.
segments.visual_prompt: person reacting instantly then pausing to think, vertical

segments.voiceover: When you're tired or stressed, System 2 shuts off first, and System 1 makes all your decisions, badly.
segments.visual_prompt: exhausted person making a rushed decision late at night, vertical

segments.voiceover: You have two brains, and the tired one is in charge right now. Now go make your big decisions after you rest.
segments.visual_prompt: person calmly deciding something after a good night's sleep, vertical

caption: This is why 2am decisions are almost always the wrong ones. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why What You Wear Changes How You Think
This Is Why Uniforms Actually Work
Your Clothes Are Changing Your Brain

segments.voiceover: Put on a lab coat, and people actually perform better on focus tests. The clothing itself changes your brain.
segments.visual_prompt: person putting on a lab coat before working, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called enclothed cognition.
segments.visual_prompt: close up of hands buttoning a formal jacket, vertical

segments.voiceover: What you wear carries symbolic meaning, and your brain shifts behavior to match that meaning, automatically.
segments.visual_prompt: person standing taller after changing into formal clothes, vertical

segments.voiceover: That's why dressing sharp for a meeting actually makes you sharper, not just more presentable.
segments.visual_prompt: person confidently walking into an office in sharp clothing, vertical

segments.voiceover: The coat changes your brain, not just your look. Now go dress like the version of you that gets it done.
segments.visual_prompt: person choosing an outfit in front of a mirror, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: DRESS AS THE PERSON YOU WANT TO BE

caption: This is a real reason 'dress for the job you want' actually works. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why Yawns And Moods Are Both Contagious
This Is Why One Person Can Ruin A Room
Your Emotions Are Not Fully Your Own

segments.voiceover: One person walks into a room stressed, and within minutes, everyone else feels it too. Nobody said a word.
segments.visual_prompt: person entering a calm office and everyone tensing up, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called emotional contagion.
segments.visual_prompt: ripple effect spreading across water, vertical

segments.voiceover: We unconsciously mimic the facial expressions and tone of people around us, and that mimicry produces the actual feeling in us.
segments.visual_prompt: group of people's facial expressions shifting together, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: YOU MIMIC, THEN YOU FEEL IT TOO

segments.voiceover: It's the same reason yawning spreads across a room, and why calm people can quietly calm down everyone near them.
segments.visual_prompt: person yawning causing others nearby to yawn too, vertical

segments.voiceover: Nobody said a word, and the whole room changed anyway. Now think about whose mood you caught today.
segments.visual_prompt: calm person smiling, spreading calm energy in a room, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: WHOSE MOOD DID YOU CATCH TODAY?

caption: This is why one calm person can fix an entire tense room. #psychologyfacts

title_options: Why You Can't Even Trust Your Own Choices
This Experiment Will Mess With Your Head
You Might Not Know Why You Chose Anything

segments.voiceover: Researchers secretly swapped people's chosen photo for a different one. Most people didn't notice, and defended the swap.
segments.visual_prompt: person choosing between two photos on a table, vertical

segments.voiceover: It's called choice blindness.
segments.visual_prompt: magic trick style card swap close up, vertical

segments.voiceover: We're often unaware of the real reasons behind our choices, so we happily invent explanations for choices we never actually made.
segments.visual_prompt: person confidently explaining a decision, thought bubble questioning it, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: WE INVENT REASONS AFTER THE FACT

segments.voiceover: It reveals something uncomfortable, your sense of 'why I chose this' might just be a story you tell after the fact.
segments.visual_prompt: person writing a journal entry justifying a decision, vertical

segments.voiceover: They swapped the answer, and people defended it anyway. Now think, do you actually know why you picked your last choice?
segments.visual_prompt: person pausing thoughtfully mid-decision, vertical
segments.on_screen_text: DO YOU KNOW WHY YOU CHOSE IT?

caption: This experiment proves your brain lies to you about your own choices. #psychologyfacts
